purpose: Test whether a stronger Intel ownership case can rest on customer economics without raising forecasts by assertion. Supplement to the broader customer decision study; not a new experiment or independent interview.

sources.observation: Intel IT reports a production migration from 2nd- to 5th-generation Xeon, 82% fewer licensed cores and six-month hardware payback. Memory increased from 768GB to 1,500GB. Live replicas allowed 7–20 second failover. Utilization targets stayed at 50–60%.
sources.limitations: Internal Intel measurements, not an independent buyer sample. No disclosed AMD alternative, total fleet scale, raw measurements or procurement prices. Improvements combine CPU, memory and consolidation. Xeon 6 benefit is expected, not measured in that migration. No chip margin or outside Intel order is established.

sources.locator: SQL Server licensing models / Per Core licensing
sources.observation: Microsoft distinguishes per-core and Server+CAL models. Physical per-core licensing counts cores subject to minimums; VM licensing has separate conditions. Thus fewer cores can matter economically in specific contracts.
sources.limitations: The guidance does not replace customer contractual terms. Do not assume every database workload, VM or cloud instance has the same licensing economics.

sources.observation: AMD also markets per-core license savings through higher-throughput CPUs and consolidation. Its example contrasts one- and two-socket AMD configurations with a two-socket 5th-gen Xeon configuration.
sources.limitations: Vendor-run TPC-H-derived workload explicitly not compliant with all published TPC-H benchmark requirements. Memory, storage and other configurations differ; security mitigations are off. This is a rival economic proposition, not independent proof that AMD wins every customer or a matched Xeon 6 comparison.

investment_inferences: Premium CPU pricing can be rational when it reduces total buyer cost, including software, energy and migration. This is more durable reasoning than shortage alone.

The appropriate ceiling is savings relative to the next-best available system, not savings relative to an obsolete server. A five-year-old Intel comparison cannot establish present Intel pricing power against AMD or Arm.
Supplier value capture remains unmeasured: customer savings may go to software vendors, OEMs, memory suppliers or the buyer. They do not automatically become Intel operating profit.

Refresh demand is not one-for-one replacement demand. More performance per socket can reduce sockets needed for the same work. Aggregate CPU units require workload growth, utilization, cores/socket, sockets/server and retirement assumptions.

A fleet can rationally retain Intel for licensed or certified workloads while migrating other jobs. Weighted customer economics, not a single successful case, would be needed to support a 40% aggregate mature DCAI margin.
forecast_action: No forecast or target change. Retain as supporting mechanism and counterexample to a simplistic replacement-volume bridge. Further work is valuable only if it estimates a material customer mix or relative system-cost advantage.
